ourClaims.studySummary: DHA is essential for brain development and maintenance. Observational studies consistently link higher omega-3 intake to reduced cognitive decline risk. However, RCT results are mixed: a 2012 Cochrane review found no benefit of omega-3 supplementation for preventing cognitive decline in healthy elderly. More targeted research (Yurko-Mauro et al., 2010) showed 900mg DHA/day improved episodic memory in age-related cognitive decline. Benefits are most consistent in populations with low baseline omega-3 status and existing cognitive concerns.

humanEffects.notes: 900mg DHA/day showed episodic memory improvements in adults with age-related cognitive concerns (Yurko-Mauro et al., 2010).
Less consistent in healthy young adults. Benefits may be most pronounced in those with low baseline omega-3 intake.
EPA component shows stronger antidepressant effect than DHA alone. Combined EPA+DHA at >1g/day shows modest mood benefits.
Higher DHA blood levels correlate with larger hippocampal volume in longitudinal MRI studies. Protective against age-related brain atrophy.

sideEffects: Mild GI discomfort at high doses
Potential blood-thinning effect at very high doses (>3g/day)

howToTake.forms: Fish oil, krill oil, algal oil

studies.title: Beneficial effects of docosahexaenoic acid on cognition in age-related cognitive decline.
studies.design: RCT, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site (19 US sites)
studies.population: Healthy adults ≥55y, MMSE>26, Logical Memory ≥1 SD below younger norms (age-related cognitive decline)
studies.outcome: CANTAB Paired Associate Learning (PAL) errors; Verbal Recognition Memory
studies.result: Significantly fewer PAL six-pattern errors with DHA vs placebo (p=0.03); improved immediate/delayed Verbal Recognition Memory (p<0.02); no effect on working memory or executive function. Plasma DHA doubled and correlated with PAL improvement. No serious treatment-related adverse events.
studies.fundingConflict: Sponsored by Martek Biosciences Corporation (an algal-DHA manufacturer); lead author is a Martek employee. Direct industry funding and authorship.

studies.title: DHA supplementation improved both memory and reaction time in healthy young adults: a randomized controlled trial.
studies.population: Healthy adults, 18–45y, nonsmoking, low habitual DHA intake
studies.outcome: Computerized cognitive battery: episodic/working memory, attention, reaction time
studies.result: Reaction time of episodic memory improved (mean diff -0.18 SD, p=0.02) and working memory RT improved (-0.36 SD, p=0.002) vs placebo. Sex-specific effects: episodic memory improved in women, working-memory RT improved in men. No effect of APOE genotype. This is the strongest healthy-adult positive RCT found, at a dose above our stated 500–1000mg range.

studies.title: Omega 3 fatty acid for the prevention of cognitive decline and dementia.
studies.dose: Varied across 3 pooled trials (gel capsules or margarine spread, omega-3 PUFA)
studies.outcome: MMSE and other cognitive tests; incident dementia (not measured in any pooled trial)
studies.result: No benefit of omega-3 PUFA supplementation on cognitive function in cognitively healthy older adults (MMSE mean difference -0.07, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.10). No trial measured incident dementia directly. Main side effect: mild GI problems in <15% of participants, balanced across arms.

studies.title: Effect of Long-Term Marine ɷ-3 Fatty Acids Supplementation on the Risk of Atrial Fibrillation in Randomized Controlled Trials of Cardiovascular Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
studies.design: Systematic review / meta-analysis of cardiovascular RCTs
studies.dose: Stratified by ≤1g/day (72.6% of pooled patients) vs >1g/day (27.4%)
studies.result: Omega-3 supplementation associated with increased AF risk overall (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.07–1.46). Risk was dose-dependent: HR 1.49 (95% CI 1.04–2.15) for >1g/day vs HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.03–1.22) for ≤1g/day; meta-regression showed HR increased 11% per additional 1g/day. This is a safety signal not mentioned anywhere on our ingredient page.
studies.fundingConflict: NIH-funded (Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural); independent academic meta-analysis.

studies.title: Cognitive efficacy of omega-3 fatty acids in Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.result: Non-significant effect on ADAS-Cog (mean difference 1.37, 95% CI 0.00–2.73, z=1.96, p=0.05) — borderline null. Omega-3 does not meaningfully help cognition once dementia (AD) has developed, distinct from the age-related-decline (pre-dementia) population where Yurko-Mauro showed benefit.

studies.title: A High Omega-3 Fatty Acid Multinutrient Supplement Benefits Cognition and Mobility in Older Women: A Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Pilot Study.
studies.dose: 1g DHA + 160mg EPA + 240mg Ginkgo biloba + 60mg PS + vitamin E/B12/folic acid (multi-ingredient, not DHA alone)
studies.outcome: Motor screening task, word recall, walking speed (VICON motion capture)
studies.result: Significant improvement in 2 of 4 cognitive tests and 1 of 3 mobility measures vs placebo; higher blood DHA levels confirmed compliance. Small pilot (n=27) and cannot isolate DHA's independent contribution from the other ingredients.
studies.fundingConflict: Not stated in retrieved abstract; tested product is a named commercial formulation (Efalex Active 50+).

verdicts.claim: Memory (Age-Related Decline) — evidenceStrength: moderate, studies: 10, anchored to Yurko-Mauro 2010
verdicts.reason: Yurko-Mauro 2010 (n=485, well-powered, industry-funded but methodologically solid RCT) does show significant PAL and verbal recognition memory improvement at 900mg/day DHA over 24 weeks, matching the claim's specific citation. The broader 'moderate, 10 studies' framing is plausible but not fully re-verified study-by-study in this session.

verdicts.claim: studySummary — 'a 2012 Cochrane review found no benefit... in healthy elderly'
verdicts.reason: Accurately represents Sydenham/Cochrane 2012: no benefit on MMSE or other cognitive tests in cognitively healthy older adults across 4,080 pooled participants. This is the one claim in the DHA page that is stated with appropriate nuance already.

verdicts.claim: Memory (Healthy Adults) — evidenceStrength: mixed, magnitude: small, studies: 8
verdicts.reason: Stonehouse 2013 (n=176, 6-month RCT, the best-designed healthy-adult trial found) showed statistically significant reaction-time improvements at a dose (1.16g/day) above our stated range, with moderate effect sizes (-0.18 to -0.36 SD) — not merely 'small.' Labeling this 'mixed/small' undersells one of the more rigorous trials in the healthy-population literature, though the sex-specific split (women vs men benefiting on different measures) does add real heterogeneity.

verdicts.claim: sideEffects — no mention of atrial fibrillation risk at higher doses
verdicts.reason: A large, NIH-funded, dose-stratified meta-analysis (n=81,210) found omega-3 supplementation significantly increases AF risk, with risk rising with dose (HR 1.49 at >1g/day). Our page's sideEffects list mentions 'blood-thinning at very high doses (>3g/day)' but omits AF entirely — a real cardiac safety signal that becomes relevant well within commonly recommended combined EPA+DHA dosing (our own howToTake suggests up to 2g/day total omega-3).

Both positive RCTs found (Yurko-Mauro 2010, Stonehouse 2013) ran 24 weeks (~6 months), not 8–12 weeks; the Cochrane review's null trials ran even longer (up to 40 months). No trial in this search demonstrated a positive cognitive effect within an 8–12 week window specifically — the FAQ text elsewhere on the page ('most RCTs... ran 12-24 weeks') is closer to accurate than the structured timeToEffect field.

doseAssessment.trialRange: 900mg/day DHA (Yurko-Mauro, ARCD population) to 1.16g/day DHA (Stonehouse, healthy adults); combination-formula trials used 1g DHA + additional ingredients
doseAssessment.ourDoseWithinRange: Roughly, but at the low end — both positive human RCTs found used doses at or above 900mg/day, near or above the top of our stated 500–1000mg range, not the middle or low end.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Consider narrowing the effective range toward 900mg–1.2g/day DHA specifically, since both positive trials cluster there, and add the AFib dose-response signal as a ceiling consideration for anyone combining DHA with EPA toward the page's suggested 1–2g/day total omega-3.

safetySignals.signal: Omega-3 supplementation significantly increases atrial fibrillation risk in a large dose-stratified meta-analysis of cardiovascular RCTs, with risk roughly 50% higher at doses >1g/day — a finding absent from the page's sideEffects list.

gaps: No trial found isolating an 8–12 week cognitive effect window; all positive trials ran ~24 weeks or longer.
The claimed hippocampal-volume/brain-structure MRI correlation (6 studies) was not independently re-verified with PMIDs in this session.
The claimed 15-study mood/depression evidence base and EPA-vs-DHA differential were not independently re-verified with PMIDs in this session.
No head-to-head trial found comparing algal vs fish-sourced DHA bioequivalence for cognitive endpoints specifically.
